title: India's Free HPV Vaccination Drive Crosses Five Months With Strong Uptake
excerpt: The nationwide campaign launched in February has vaccinated millions of 14-year-old girls across all states, with Karnataka among the states reporting surging demand at government health centres.
body:
• India launched its free HPV vaccination campaign on 28 February 2026, targeting 1.2 crore girls aged 14 across all 36 states and union territories
  • The single-dose Gardasil-4 vaccine, procured through a partnership with Gavi, is administered at government health facilities free of cost
  • Cervical cancer kills an estimated 80,000 Indian women annually — the vaccine is 93–100% effective in preventing HPV-linked cancers

Five months into India's largest preventive health campaign, the free HPV vaccination drive is reporting strong uptake across the country, with several states — Karnataka among them — seeing sustained demand at government health centres.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched the nationwide Human Papillomavirus vaccination campaign on 28 February 2026, incorporating it into India's Universal Immunisation Programme. The drive targets approximately 1.2 crore (12 million) girls aged 14, offering them a single dose of the Gardasil-4 vaccine at no cost, according to the Press Information Bureau.

Context

India accounts for roughly a quarter of global cervical cancer deaths, with an estimated 1.2 lakh new cases and 80,000 deaths each year. Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer among Indian women, and the vast majority of cases are linked to persistent infection with high-risk HPV strains, particularly types 16 and 18.

The government's decision to offer free vaccination followed years of deliberation. The National Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation (NTAGI) and the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) both endorsed the single-dose strategy after reviewing WHO recommendations. Ninety countries, including most of Southeast Asia, have adopted single-dose HPV vaccination schedules.

"The government has focussed on starting with the upper age to make sure that they are vaccinated before they turn 15. We have received 1.5 crore doses till now out of the promised 2.6 crore doses by Gavi."

— Dr Abhishek Shanker, Oncologist, AIIMS New Delhi

The vaccine is procured through India's partnership with Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, which committed $250 million in 2023 to strengthen India's health systems. Gardasil-4, manufactured by Merck, protects against HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18.

How the Drive Works

The initial phase ran as a 90-day mission-mode campaign with daily vaccine availability at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, primary health centres, community health centres, district hospitals, and government medical colleges. Each session is supervised by a medical officer and linked to a 24/7 hospital for adverse event management. Parental consent is mandatory.

In Karnataka, the programme was launched at K.C. General Hospital in Bengaluru via a webcast of the national event. State health officials began field-level awareness campaigns to encourage eligible families, and the Health Department has indicated plans to expand coverage further in the coming months, according to local reports.

Digital infrastructure plays a central role. Parents register through the U-WIN platform, and the Electronic Vaccine Intelligence Network (eVIN) tracks vaccine stocks and cold-chain temperatures in real time. Each vaccinated girl receives a digital certificate with emergency contact details.

Impact

Medical evidence shows the Gardasil vaccine is 93–100% effective in preventing cervical cancer when administered before exposure to the virus. Over 500 million HPV vaccine doses have been administered globally since 2006, with surveillance by the WHO and the US CDC confirming a strong safety profile.

The campaign aligns with the WHO's 90-70-90 targets for 2030: 90% of girls vaccinated, 70% of women screened, and 90% of those diagnosed receiving treatment. By pairing adolescent vaccination with screening for women aged 30–65, India is shifting from managing cervical cancer to working toward its elimination.

For India's diaspora, the drive marks a public health milestone. HPV vaccination has been standard in countries like the US, UK, and Australia for over a decade. India's nationwide adoption — making the vaccine free and voluntary — puts it on par with global best practices. Families visiting India or sending daughters to study there now have access to the same preventive care available in Western health systems, and those considering CERVAVAC, India's indigenous HPV vaccine by the Serum Institute, can access it privately for ₹1,200–1,700 per dose.

What's Next

After the initial 90-day push concluded in late May, the vaccine has been integrated into routine weekly immunisation sessions. The government expects to receive the remaining 1.1 crore doses of the 2.6 crore promised by Gavi in the coming months.

Health officials have signalled plans to expand the programme's reach, potentially extending catch-up vaccination to older age groups. The broader goal is to build on India's COVID-era digital vaccination infrastructure — from CoWIN to U-WIN — to sustain high coverage rates well beyond the initial campaign.
